rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and the few insects measured see far less fine detail than that. If you are a common green darner you see about a fifteenth as much as a human, and if you are an orange sulphur about a fortieth. If you are an Old World swallowtail, a table compiled from the literature gives about a fiftieth, and for most other insects nobody has measured how sharply you see.
rows.note: Gave sharpness as fractions of a human's 30 cycles a degree instead of decimals; left out the facet-angle figures and the other measured species.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: A human stops seeing a light as flickering at about 60 flashes a second, and the butterflies measured so far see flicker well beyond that. Danaus chrysippus, a close relative of the monarch, responds to flicker at 160 to 210 flashes a second, and the skipper Epargyreus clarus at 180 to 200. Nobody has measured how fast you see flicker if you are a ladybird beetle, a stink bug, a dragonfly, or one of most of the other butterflies.
rows.note: Left out the drone fly corner frequency (R9) and the dragonfly ocellus value (R28): neither states how fast a compound eye follows flicker.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In the monarch, the cabbage white, the small tortoiseshell, the drone fly, the seven-spotted ladybird beetle and the green darner dragonfly, one kind of color-sensing cell is most sensitive to ultraviolet, and you very likely have such a cell too.
rows.note: Left out spectral-range claims: no record gives a range for most species here, and dragonflies have none.
